_about: How the kind of writing changes how its language works. Catholic teaching asks readers to attend to literary genres (Dei Verbum 12).

entries.title: Creation account
entries.note: The text is carefully patterned: two triads of days (forming and filling) and a Sabbath. The Church has never taught that it is a scientific description of how the world began; it teaches that everything depends on God and is good. Genre is discussed in the Catechism (CCC 337-342) and in Dei Verbum 12, which asks readers to attend to the literary forms the sacred writers used.

entries.title: Primeval narrative
entries.note: A narrative in symbolic language about the origin of humanity, sin and death. The Catechism says Genesis 3 uses figurative language but affirms a primeval event (CCC 390).

entries.title: Patriarchal narrative
entries.note: Stories of families told with a theological interest in promise and covenant. Dates and some details cannot be settled from outside sources.

entries.title: Law (apodictic)
entries.note: The Ten Words are a short, unconditional list of commands that open the covenant. They are not case law ('if someone does X') in the way much of Exodus 21-23 is.

entries.title: Case law
entries.note: Laws written in 'if... then' form, like other ancient Near Eastern collections. They set limits and penalties in the context of their own society and are read by the Church in the light of Christ (CCC 1961-1964).

entries.title: Ritual instruction
entries.note: The priests' handbook on offerings. The detail is the point: it teaches that approach to God is ordered by what God has given.

entries.title: Historical narrative with theological shaping
entries.note: The conquest narratives use stylised language ('utterly destroyed'). Interpreters, ancient and modern, discuss how literally to take such totalising language.

entries.title: Historical narrative with a refrain
entries.note: The refrain 'in those days there was no king in Israel' frames the stories as a warning.

entries.title: Wisdom drama
entries.note: A poem set in a prose frame. It is a long argument about suffering and not a report of a conversation. The speeches of Job's friends contain statements that God finally says are wrong (Job 42:7).

entries.title: Hebrew poetry
entries.note: The psalms are poetry in which the line is built on parallelism: the second line repeats, intensifies or contrasts the first. Read the pair, not just one half, and notice that the language is prayer, not argument.

entries.title: Lament
entries.note: A psalm of lament that includes a cry for vengeance. The Liturgy of the Hours omits the most violent verses, and the tradition has read such language as the honest prayer of the wounded, handed over to God.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.note: Proverbs state general patterns, not promises. 'Train up a child in the way he should go' (22:6) describes how things usually go; it is not a guarantee for every family.

entries.title: Wisdom reflection
entries.note: The speaker (Qoheleth) tests everything 'under the sun' and finds it fleeting (hebel, 'breath'). The book is a reflection that asks the reader to see the limits of human wisdom, and its conclusion is in 12:13-14.

entries.title: Love poetry
entries.note: Love poems that the Jewish and Christian traditions have both read as speaking of God's love for his people, and the Church's tradition as Christ and the Church or the soul. The literal sense is love between a man and woman.

entries.title: Prophetic oracle
entries.note: Prophetic speech is poetry that mixes warning and promise. It is not usually prediction in a simple sense; it speaks to the prophet's own time and is read in the New Testament as also pointing to Christ.

entries.title: Prophetic sign-oracle
entries.note: A sign given to a king in a political crisis. How it also speaks of Christ is discussed in the Gospel of Matthew (1:23).

entries.title: Prophetic narrative
entries.note: A short story with irony and exaggeration, with a message about God's mercy to enemies. Catholic scholars have read it as a historical narrative and as a didactic story; the Church has not settled that question.

entries.title: Apocalyptic
entries.note: A vision-writing that uses symbolic animals, numbers and heavenly figures to say that God rules history under persecution. It is not a timetable.

entries.title: Apocalyptic letter
entries.note: A prophetic letter to seven churches in symbolic, liturgical imagery drawn from the Old Testament. Numbers and creatures are symbols. The imagery speaks to Christians under persecution and about the end.

entries.title: Hyperbole
entries.note: Jesus uses exaggeration to make a point about the seriousness of sin. The tradition has never taken the command to cut off the hand as a literal command.

entries.title: Parables
entries.note: Parables are stories that make one main point, and the details usually do not each stand for something. They should be read in their Gospel context and with the explanations the Gospel itself gives.

entries.title: Genealogy
entries.note: A genealogy in the ancient style: it selects names, groups them (here in three sets of fourteen) and says something about Jesus as son of David and son of Abraham. It is not a complete list.

entries.title: Gospel (ancient biography with theological purpose)
entries.note: The Gospels are not diaries; they gather and arrange what Jesus said and did for particular communities (Dei Verbum 19). That explains why accounts differ in order and wording.

entries.title: Preface to a historical work
entries.note: A preface in the manner of Greek historians, in which Luke says he has investigated and set events in order for Theophilus.

entries.title: Historical monograph
entries.note: A narrative of the early Church with speeches, summaries and travel accounts. The speeches are summaries composed by the author.

entries.title: Letter
entries.note: A letter written as an argument to a community. Read it as a whole before taking a single verse; Paul's words often answer an objection that is only implied.

entries.title: Homily
entries.note: This 'word of exhortation' (13:22) is closer to a sermon than a letter, built on a chain of Old Testament quotations.

entries.title: Wisdom exhortation
entries.note: A string of short teachings, like the Old Testament wisdom books, with the Gospel of Matthew's Sermon on the Mount echoing in the background.

entries.title: Historical story
entries.note: A story told with irony and reversal. The Greek additions give the book the explicit religious language that the Hebrew lacks.

entries.title: Pious narrative
entries.note: A family story with angels, a demon and a journey. It is taught as inspired Scripture in the Catholic canon, and read for its message of prayer and almsgiving.

entries.title: Historical fiction (debated)
entries.note: The book has deliberate historical errors, such as calling Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians, which signal a story with a message. The Church does not require any particular answer.

entries.title: Wasf (body-description poetry)
entries.note: A description of the beloved's body in imagery of landscape and animals. The images are metaphors, and a literal reading misses the point.
